# Code style (pokedex Python)

The always-on subset, consolidated from CLAUDE.md and `integration-patterns.md` "Code style". Full reviewer checklist (incl. advisory / new-build-only items like `while True`, guard clauses, inline dict values): `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Code style".

- **No docstrings, with two exceptions.** Pokedex code is self-documenting. Both exceptions are where the docstring is published text, not a comment: `api.py` endpoint handlers, whose docstring is the endpoint's OpenAPI summary and description (the rollout pushes that spec to Mintlify and Svix, so it is the public API docs, and every public endpoint carries one); Alembic migration modules under `migrations/versions/`, which keep the generated header (title, `Revision ID`, `Revises`, `Create Date`) plus a line of rationale when the schema change is not obvious from the operations. Nothing under `integrations/`, `utils/`, `resources/`, or `actions/` has one.
- **Default to no comment; when in doubt, delete.** A comment exists only when the change is not obvious from the code alone. If the code, a variable name, or the error message beside it already says it, the comment is noise — delete it rather than polish it. That covers narration ("sum the quantities per sku"), section labels, and anything restating an assert or a raise.
- **Comments: lowercase, ≤2 lines, why not what.** Vendor quirks, surprising invariants, non-obvious couplings. Vendor field names keep their original casing inside a lowercase comment (`DeliveryNotes` stays `DeliveryNotes`) — lowercasing them breaks the reference. The ceiling yields only when a genuinely non-obvious vendor data model or a disambiguating example needs the room and nothing shorter carries it. The same ceiling applies to raised error messages — a `PokedexException` says what went wrong and what to do in a line or two, not a paragraph.
- **ELI5, no jargon.** Write it the way you'd say it out loud to an engineer new to the codebase: plain words any SWE understands cold, in one read. No noun-stacks ("multi-lot pick collision"), no arrow chains (`x → y → z`), no model-speak ("ensure correctness", "for clarity", "leverage"), no clever compression that needs decoding ("must not look like it did"). "with no batch number, picks from different batches get combined here, so we can't keep a single expiry date" beats "blank-batch multi-lot picks collapse under the package uniqueness key, dropping the expiry anchor".
- **Comments are self-contained.** Never reference `api-summary.md`, any `.claude/...` file, doctrine vocabulary ("tier-3", "shallow-fix", "per integration-patterns"), or the authoring agent. A reader at HEAD with only this file open must understand it.
- **Comments never name** customer orgs, the source integration a pattern was copied from, or observation dates — those leak or rot. The ban is on customers: naming the integration's own vendor inside its own files is normal. Rich rationale (customer, pattern source, load-bearing dates) lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Exception: vendor/3PL support-contact lines inside `support()` — naming contacts is that method's job.
- **Raise, don't `assert`.** Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` exception helpers), never `assert` — asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status or origin. `assert` belongs in tests only.
- **A package `__init__.py` that re-exports lists those names in `__all__`.** Re-exports are the point of the file, but every one of them reads as an unused import to the linter, so the list is what keeps it quiet and doubles as the package's public surface. Add a name in both places or the linter flags it again.
- **No `@property` on anything a subclass overrides.** A value an integration can change is a plain method, so every call site shows it's dispatched rather than read off the instance. `@property` is still fine for something defined once and never overridden (`staging_key`, `bucket`). Name a boolean method for how it reads at the call site — `uses_browserbase()`, not `use_browserbase()`.
- **No `ABC` / `@abstractmethod`.** A base class declares a method subclasses must supply by raising `NotImplementedError` in the body, with a short message saying what the subclass owes. That's the one pattern used everywhere else, and on integrations it's load-bearing: `BaseIntegration.is_implemented` reads a method's source looking for that raise to decide which functions an integration supports, so an abstract stub would be read as implemented and get scheduled.
- **UPPER_CASE names are module-level only.** A constant-style value scoped inside a function is a lowercase local like any other; capitals are reserved for module-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor tunables).
- **No leading-underscore "private" names** on methods, attributes, or locals. Underscore privacy isn't enforced here and signals nothing. If a class helper needs `self` it's a method; if not, hoist it module-level; if used once, inline it. (Dunders like `__init__` are exempt.)
- **Error-driven: avoid `.get()` — on vendor-response reads.** Loud failures (a `KeyError` during `yarn crawl`) are how we learn real API behavior. `.get(field, default)` on a vendor response is allowed only after observing the field is genuinely sometimes-absent. Nullable is not optional: a key the vendor always sends but sometimes nulls is read with a direct index (plus an `or` fallback when a default is needed) — `.get()` there misstates the contract by implying the key can be missing. The rule does not cover reads where absence is the normal, documented case — optional fields of a validated write payload in `create_*`/`update_*` methods, marshmallow `query_data` in API handlers (absent optional params are omitted from the dict), and our own state attributes that most rows don't carry — there `.get()` is the convention and is self-documenting. Comment a `.get()` only when the absence is surprising (the contract says the field should be there and observation proved otherwise: `# vendor returns null for unfulfilled orders`); a `.get()` on a documented-optional field needs no comment.
- **No list/dict comprehensions in integration code.** Use multi-line `for` loops with named intermediates — comprehensions are opaque under `pdb`.
- **No `logger.info` / `print` in integration code** (carrier is the documented exception — its async/queued flows justify checkpoint logging). Every other type stays quiet: Datadog spans + connection-error rows are the observability surface; `logger.warning`/`error` only for genuinely surprising, actionable states.
- **Platform constants live in `config.py`.** Feature modules `import config`; don't scatter `os.environ.get`. Integration-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor base URLs, per-vendor tunables) stay in the integration's own module — they're hard to unify across vendors and don't belong in the shared config.
- **Favor simplicity over cleverness — and the smallest fix that addresses the root cause.** A fix that adds new mechanisms (a helper, a wrapper, a retry layer, config) where editing an existing line suffices is overengineered and gets rejected in review. Before inventing a new shape, check how neighboring integrations already solve the same problem and match it. The same bar applies to edge cases: a narrow race or double-failure edge that self-corrects on the next cycle (or whose outcome is still correct for the user) is documented — or made observable with a log line — not engineered around with new state machines or guards.

- **Reuse the codebase's words; never coin a verb.** A name is found, not composed: before naming a function, helper, constant, status value, or table, grep for how neighbors name the same operation on the same kind of thing (`rg -n 'def \w+_<noun>\b'`, `rg -n 'def \w+_row\b'`) and pick from the verbs that come back; the search is by object, never by a list of verbs, because a list is itself a vocabulary that drifts. Dynamo row helpers are `create_ / get_ / update_ / store_ / delete_<thing>_row`. Under `integrations/`, data-function and action names come from the resource and action contracts, so there is nothing to choose. A status string is the word the API's error text uses for that state (`unconfirmed` when the 409 says "could not be confirmed"), so the row, the log line, and the error read the same. A word from one recent feature is not established vocabulary; count its uses across the repo before adopting it. Payments, ops, and distributed-systems jargon (`settle`, `claim`, `release`, `landed`, `in flight`, `ambiguous`, `reconcile`) is a coined verb here unless the grep shows it already carries that meaning in this codebase. Say what the code does in words the code already uses: `mark_<row>_succeeded`, `store_write_ids_for_replay`, `write_may_have_reached_vendor`.
- **Comments and error messages use the code's own names.** A comment names the function, status, and field exactly as the code spells them and describes the mechanism in the same verbs. A comment that introduces a second vocabulary for the thing beside it is rewritten in the code's words or deleted.

## Running code & tests
- **Tests: only `yarn test` with filters.** Never `python -m pytest` or raw `pytest`. Scopes/markers: `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md`.
- **Ad-hoc Python: `uv run python3`.** Never raw `python3`/`python` — dependencies resolve through `uv`.

Both exceptions are where the docstring is published text, not a comment: `api.py` endpoint handlers, whose docstring is the endpoint's OpenAPI summary and description (the rollout pushes that spec to Mintlify and Svix, so it is the public API docs, and every public endpoint carries one); Alembic migration modules under `migrations/versions/`, which keep the generated header (title, `Revision ID`, `Revises`, `Create Date`) plus a line of rationale when the schema change is not obvious from the operations. Nothing under `integrations/`, `utils/`, `resources/`, or `actions/` has one.
- **Default to no comment; when in doubt, delete.** A comment exists only when the change is not obvious from the code alone. If the code, a variable name, or the error message beside it already says it, the comment is noise — delete it rather than polish it. That covers narration ("sum the quantities per sku"), section labels, and anything restating an assert or a raise.
- **Comments: lowercase, ≤2 lines, why not what.** Vendor quirks, surprising invariants, non-obvious couplings. Vendor field names keep their original casing inside a lowercase comment (`DeliveryNotes` stays `DeliveryNotes`) — lowercasing them breaks the reference. The ceiling yields only when a genuinely non-obvious vendor data model or a disambiguating example needs the room and nothing shorter carries it. The same ceiling applies to raised error messages — a `PokedexException` says what went wrong and what to do in a line or two, not a paragraph.
- **ELI5, no jargon.** Write it the way you'd say it out loud to an engineer new to the codebase: plain words any SWE understands cold, in one read. No noun-stacks ("multi-lot pick collision"), no arrow chains (`x → y → z`), no model-speak ("ensure correctness", "for clarity", "leverage"), no clever compression that needs decoding ("must not look like it did"). "with no batch number, picks from different batches get combined here, so we can't keep a single expiry date" beats "blank-batch multi-lot picks collapse under the package uniqueness key, dropping the expiry anchor".
- **Comments are self-contained.** Never reference `api-summary.md`, any `.claude/...` file, doctrine vocabulary ("tier-3", "shallow-fix", "per integration-patterns"), or the authoring agent. A reader at HEAD with only this file open must understand it.
- **Comments never name** customer orgs, the source integration a pattern was copied from, or observation dates — those leak or rot. The ban is on customers: naming the integration's own vendor inside its own files is normal. Rich rationale (customer, pattern source, load-bearing dates) lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Exception: vendor/3PL support-contact lines inside `support()` — naming contacts is that method's job.
- **Raise, don't `assert`.** Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` exception helpers), never `assert` — asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status or origin. `assert` belongs in tests only.
- **A package `__init__.py` that re-exports lists those names in `__all__`.** Re-exports are the point of the file, but every one of them reads as an unused import to the linter, so the list is what keeps it quiet and doubles as the package's public surface. - **No `@property` on anything a subclass overrides.** A value an integration can change is a plain method, so every call site shows it's dispatched rather than read off the instance. `@property` is still fine for something defined once and never overridden (`staging_key`, `bucket`). - **UPPER_CASE names are module-level only.** A constant-style value scoped inside a function is a lowercase local like any other; capitals are reserved for module-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor tunables).

Nullable is not optional: a key the vendor always sends but sometimes nulls is read with a direct index (plus an `or` fallback when a default is needed) — `.get()` there misstates the contract by implying the key can be missing. - **No `logger.info` / `print` in integration code** (carrier is the documented exception — its async/queued flows justify checkpoint logging). - **Reuse the codebase's words; never coin a verb.** A name is found, not composed: before naming a function, helper, constant, status value, or table, grep for how neighbors name the same operation on the same kind of thing (`rg -n 'def \w+_<noun>\b'`, `rg -n 'def \w+_row\b'`) and pick from the verbs that come back; the search is by object, never by a list of verbs, because a list is itself a vocabulary that drifts. A word from one recent feature is not established vocabulary; count its uses across the repo before adopting it. A comment that introduces a second vocabulary for the thing beside it is rewritten in the code's words or deleted.

## Running code & tests
- **Tests: only `yarn test` with filters.** Never `python -m pytest` or raw `pytest`. Scopes/markers: `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md`.
- **Ad-hoc Python: `uv run python3`.** Never raw `python3`/`python` — dependencies resolve through `uv`.

# Write safety — never touch production vendor data

Full rules: `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Write safety". The always-on core:

- **Write methods** — `create_*`, `update_*`, `cancel_*`, `delete_*`, `adjust_*`, `refund_*` (anything that mutates vendor state) — are gated by **`allow_writes()` on the test class** (defined in `test/integrations/base_test.py`, defaults `True`; read by `write_and_validate`, which skips every write test when `False`).
- **Any connection that is not writes-safe** — prod-as-test, customer-owned, or unlabeled — the test class **MUST** override `allow_writes(self): return False`. Without the override, write tests fire against the vendor.
- **File-based integrations: `allow_file_archive()` on the test class gates the archive step** (defined in `test/integrations/base_test.py`, defaults `False`; crawl tests patch out `archive_staged_files` unless the class opts in). Archiving consumes files off the vendor's server, and on a prod or shared server that starves the customer's own crawls. Return `True` only for a sandbox or test server we're allowed to drain, per `test_account()`.
- **Don't restate the writes-safe default.** On a writes-safe connection, omit `allow_writes()` rather than writing `return True`. An explicit `True` earns its place only as a deliberate authorization record — a prod-as-test account where writes were confirmed safe — paired with a `test_account()` that says so and why.
- **`test_account()` is the human-readable rationale** for that value: `"<requesting org> <env> · <ownership> · <write-safety> · <linear-ticket>"`. The leading token is the trackstar customer org that requested the build — not `test-org-id`, not the vendor name. `test_account()` and `allow_writes()` must agree (`writes-unsafe` ↔ returns `False`). A `test-*` connection_id does **not** imply writes-safe.
- **Never run a write operation against a vendor API while investigating or validating**, regardless of account safety. HTTP method is **not** the gate — SOAP and GraphQL reads are POST; the operation's *effect on vendor data* is. Default to read-only paths: `yarn crawl` dry-run and documented read endpoints. Never change `allow_writes()` / `test_account()` to flip write-safety as a shortcut.

# Integration fidelity (what every integration must do)

An integration's job is to **faithfully represent the source API to the customer** — not to make tests pass, not to match a paper spec, not to ship without errors. Full enforcement checklist: `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` ("Format function output shape", "Inspect nested structure", "Data access", "Root-cause-first", the shallow-fix family). The always-on core:

## Doctrine
- **Loud failures > quiet workarounds.** A `KeyError` during `yarn crawl` is information; `.get(field, None)` is amnesia. Default to breaking so you can see what's happening.
- **Spec is canonical, sandbox is sample.** A field in the vendor spec but absent from your sandbox response is still real — implement it. Don't strip a field because this sample didn't echo it.
- **Decisions need rationale.** Every non-obvious field choice gets a terse self-contained code comment + a richer entry in `.claude/references/{integration}/api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions".
- **Vendor-side root cause → vendor escalation.** When investigation lands on a vendor bug, outage, or permission gap, the first move is a support ticket or permission request (draft via `/generate-support-email`), not workaround code. A workaround that must ship anyway records why in `api-summary.md`. It also needs a Linear ticket, named there, only when it is an anti-pattern here: one of the shallow-fix family below, or a shape the code-style or patterns checklist bans. A workaround that reuses what other integrations already do for the same vendor behavior, like halving the page size when the vendor times out, needs no ticket.

## Root-cause-first (mandatory order before any escape hatch)
Before reaching for `.get()`, `IntegrationNotImplemented`, a disabled validator, or a modified test:
1. Read the **raw response** (JSON/XML, not the parsed model) — what's there, what type, what value.
2. Check **other endpoints** (`/orders/{id}`, a webhook event, an `expand=` param).
3. Re-read the **spec** for params/headers/flags that change response shape.
4. Compare **sandbox vs prod** — sandbox is often impoverished; treat divergence as state, not a contract issue.
5. Check the vendor **changelog/status**.
6. **Surface to the user** with what you observed. Only then use an escape hatch — and only with recorded rationale.

## Never (shallow-fix family — each needs documented rationale to be acceptable)
- Disable a validator flag / weaken `Strict()`→`Loose()`; write a custom validator that just accepts what the canonical one rejected.
- `IntegrationNotImplemented` without investigating other endpoints/spec.
- `.get(field, default)` without an observed-missing comment.
- Modify a failing test until it passes (fix the code or escalate instead).
- Synthesize values (`now()`, hardcoded dates/strings) to satisfy a required schema field.
- Swallow exceptions silently in `except` blocks.

## Output-shape invariants
- **`IntegrationNotImplemented` vs `None`:** `IntegrationNotImplemented` = the field is structurally absent in **both** directions (no read exposes it AND no write accepts it). If even one code path provides it, all other paths use `None`. A field the vendor **accepts on write but doesn't echo on read** is `None` (with a one-line comment naming the asymmetry), not `IntegrationNotImplemented`. Exception: a canonical `List`/`Dict` field whose schema rejects `None` (its `not_implemented_default` is `[]`/`{}`, so `allow_none` never auto-enables) takes `IntegrationNotImplemented` on the read side even when a write accepts it — record the asymmetry in `api-summary.md`. Never `x = data.get(y, IntegrationNotImplemented)` or `x = y or IntegrationNotImplemented`.
- **Dates:** pull `created_date`/`updated_date` from source. If the vendor exposes only one, set the missing one equal to the present one — `created_date` is frozen on first write, so this is the one chance to record the real historical timestamp; omitting lets the pipeline backfill `EPOCH`/1970 (a customer-visible lie). Omit both only when neither is sourceable. Never synthesize `now()` / hardcoded dates on a read path. Carve-out: when the write itself creates the record, `now()` at the moment of the write is the record's true origin timestamp — stamping it there records history rather than inventing it (compute it once and reuse the same value everywhere that moment appears); omitting it freezes the 1970 epoch backfill instead.
- **`trackstar_tags`:** never populate (user-managed). **`additional_fields`:** default `{}`; populate for an explicitly requested customer field, or for a deliberate vendor-specific extra that no canonical field can carry and that downstream behavior needs — with the rationale recorded in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Never for data that has a canonical slot.
- **`[]` is not an absence value** for a structural decomposition: if a parent has data that must split across a child collection, don't ship `[]` — use the per-element breakdown, copy the parent collection to the single child, or escalate. When nothing anywhere in the API holds the data at all — no parent collection to copy, no breakdown to derive — the sanctioned mechanism is the per-integration exemption list on the canonical validator in `resources/`: extend the list rather than fabricating rows. modify_start = start
        if first_loop:
            # buffer to catch orders shipstation's api is slow to index. later loops
            # start at the last modifyDate the crawl already read, so they skip it
            modify_start = start - timedelta(hours=2)
            self.shipment_start_date = dt_to_str(start - timedelta(days=7))
        # bulk edits can stamp more orders with one modifyDate second than fit in a page,
        # so the second-based cursor stalls; page within it via a {modify_date, page} token.
        ss_page = 1
        offset = 0
        if page_token:
            if isinstance(page_token, str) and page_token.startswith("{"):
                cursor = json.loads(page_token)
                modify_start = cursor["modify_date"]
                ss_page = cursor["page"]
                offset = cursor.get("offset", 0)
            else:
                modify_start = page_token
        query_params = {
            "modifyDateStart": modify_start,
            # bound orders to end; the shipment window stops at end, so without this a
            # back-sync with a past end pulls later orders and stores them with no shipment
            "modifyDateEnd": end,
            "pageSize": page_size,
            "page": ss_page,
            "sortBy": "ModifyDate",
            "sortDir": "ASC",
        }
        orders_rsp = self.shipstation_request("orders", params=query_params)
        orders = orders_rsp["orders"]
        # modifyDate is account-local (pacific) time, so compare seconds in pacific
        if isinstance(modify_start, datetime):
            pacific_start = modify_start.astimezone(pytz.timezone("US/Pacific"))
            start_second = pacific_start.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")
        else:
            start_second = modify_start.split(".")[0]
        page_next_token = None
        page_next_start = None
        if len(orders) == page_size and not self.in_perm_validator():
            last_second = orders[-1]["modifyDate"].split(".")[0]
            last_second_dt = str_to_dt(format_date(last_second))
            # if the whole page falls in one second, re-anchoring there would refetch it,
            # so walk shipstation's page within that second
            if last_second == start_second:
                next_second = start_second
                next_page = ss_page + 1
            else:
                next_second = last_second
                next_page = 1
            # move the window forward with next_start so latest_data advances during long
            # backfills. the first loop's buffer can put last_second before start, so that stays a token
            if next_page == 1 and start < last_second_dt < end:
                page_next_start = last_second_dt
            else:
                page_next_token = json.dumps(
                    {"modify_date": next_second, "page": next_page},
                    separators=(",", ":"),
                )

        shipment_start_date = self.shipment_start_date

content.text:
ShipStation `get_orders` now advances `latest_data` during long backfills by returning `next_start`, and the page token has one shape. A live dry run works, but `yarn test` couldn't run on this machine. Nothing is committed yet.

**What changed** (`integrations/wms/shipstation/integration.py`)
- **2h buffer only on the first loop.** Later loops start at the last `modifyDate` the crawl already read. The 7-day shipment cutoff is now saved on the first loop, so later windows don't fetch orders the prefetch already covered one by one.
- **`next_start`.** When a full page ends on a later second than `start` and before `end`, it returns that second as `next_start` with no token. It still returns a token in three cases: the whole page is inside one second, the first loop's buffer puts the last second at or before `start`, or it is partway through a page (the offset slicing).
- **Timezone.** I checked this against the dev account first. ShipStation respects the UTC offset on `modifyDateStart`: `13:16:10-07:00` returned the same results as the local-time string `13:16:10`, and `+00:00` shifted the results by 7 hours. So the last `modifyDate` is converted from Pacific to UTC, the same way `format_date` does it.
- **One token shape.** The token is always a dict, `{"modify_date", "page", "offset"}`. The JSON-string and plain-string branches are gone, and so is `import json`.

**Verification**
- A dry-run `yarn crawl` over 2024-01 to now ran 4 pages of 500 orders, each starting a new window.
- A direct probe of chained calls showed `start` moving forward each page: `2025-08-21 → 2025-11-06 18:16:04 → 2025-11-24 21:16:45 → 2025-12-12 20:39:07 → 2026-01-13 16:00:48`.
- `yarn test -k shipstation --orders --gets` failed before any test ran. `api.py` can't resolve the database hostname here (`socket.gaierror` in `utils/sql.py:53`). That looks like this machine's network setup (VPN), not the change, so the tests need a rerun where the DB resolves.

**Deploy risk from the single token shape:** any crawl still holding a JSON-string token when this ships will fail on `page_token["modify_date"]`. It will keep failing on every retry, because it resumes from that stored token each time. Before deploying, either clear `latest_page_token` on ShipStation `get_orders` schedule rows that have one, or ship at a time when none are mid-crawl.

`next_start` has one more cost: after each 500-order page the crawl waits for the previous page's submits to finish before moving on. That slows backfills, but it is also what lets `latest_data` move forward during them.

content.text:
Mostly, yes. After the first loop, `modify_date` is always equal to `start`: each window begins at `next_start`, and every token it produces (paging within one second, or the offset slices) points back at that same second. The 2h buffer on the first loop is the reason it can't be dropped.

- **The first query doesn't start at `start`.** It starts at `start - 2h`. A token produced there (the offset slices, or a full page inside one second) points at the buffered second, not at `start`.
- **A full page can end inside the buffer.** If more than 500 orders were modified in the 2 hours before `start`, the page's last second is at or before `start`. It can't become `next_start`, because the crawler requires `next_start` to be after `start`. So it has to be a token that points at a time that is neither `start` nor `start - 2h`.
- **Resuming after a crash can't tell the cases apart.** The crawler resumes with `first_loop=True`, the saved token, and the window's unbuffered start. It passes the same `start` whether the token came from the buffered first window or a later unbuffered one. With only `{page, offset}` in the token, `get_orders` has to guess whether to subtract 2h. A wrong guess shifts ShipStation's page numbering by however many orders fall in those 2 hours, which skips or re-reads them.

The only way to drop `modify_date` is to replace it with something like a `buffered: true` flag, and that's no simpler. I'd keep the token as it is.

If you'd rather drop the field anyway, the change is to stop buffering when the first page is full and ends inside the buffer, which loses the buffer on busy accounts.

lastPrompt: is there a way to just do it with crawl_start_overlap?

content.text:
Yes, for the buffer itself. Setting `crawl_start_overlap_minutes = 120` on the ShipStation integration replaces the hand-rolled `start - timedelta(hours=2)`. The crawler subtracts the overlap once, when the crawl begins (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:302`), and passes `next_start` through unchanged for later windows. That is exactly "buffer only on the first loop" without any code in `get_orders`. It's integration-wide, but every other ShipStation function (`get_inventory`, `get_products`, `get_warehouses`, `get_shipping_methods`) ignores `start`, so in practice only orders feel it.

It doesn't let you drop `modify_date` from the token, though:

- **Resumes get the overlap too.** Say a window started at `next_start` = X and crashed mid-page. The crawler resumes with `start = X - 2h`, because the overlap is applied to whatever start it reads from the row. The saved `{page, offset}` was counted from X, so page N from X - 2h lands on different orders. The token has to carry the anchor it was counted from.
- **A page that ends inside the buffer still has no `next_start`.** The crawler checks `next_start` against the unbuffered start (`current_start_dt`, `crawler.py:386`), while `get_orders` receives the buffered one. On the first loop, `get_orders` would need to compare against `start + overlap` to avoid tripping `next_start is not inside the remaining crawl range`. That case also still needs a token that points at a specific second.

So with the overlap, `get_orders` loses the first-loop buffer branch but keeps `modify_date` in the token, plus a small `+ overlap` on the first-loop check. It's still simpler than what's there now, and it uses the crawler's own mechanism rather than a ShipStation-only one. I'd make that swap. Want me to?

        orders = orders_rsp["orders"]
        # modifyDate is account-local (pacific) time, so compare seconds in pacific
        if isinstance(modify_start, datetime):
            pacific_start = modify_start.astimezone(pytz.timezone("US/Pacific"))

            start_second = modify_start.split(".")[0]
        page_next_token = None
        page_next_start = None
        if len(orders) == page_size and not self.in_perm_validator():
            last_second = orders[-1]["modifyDate"].split(".")[0]
            last_second_dt = str_to_dt(format_date(last_second))
            # if the whole page falls in one second, re-anchoring there would refetch it,

                next_page = 1
            # move the window forward with next_start so latest_data advances during long

            if next_page == 1 and start < last_second_dt < end:

                    "offset": 0,

content.text:
`modify_start` is now always one type. It's split into two variables:

- **`modify_start_dt`** is always an aware datetime. It comes from `start`, from `start - 2h` on the first loop, or from `str_to_dt(format_date(page_token["modify_date"]))` when there's a token.
- **`modify_start_str`** is always derived from it: the Pacific whole second. It is used for the query, for the same-second comparison, and as the token's `modify_date`.

The `isinstance` branch and `start_second` are gone.

The query now sends the Pacific whole second instead of the datetime. That way a page and any token that points back at it run exactly the same query. It relies on the account's local time being Pacific. `format_date` already assumes that, and the token path has always sent Pacific strings.

The probe gives the same windows as before: `2025-08-21 → 2025-11-06 18:16:04 → 2025-11-24 21:16:45`. I also resumed from a token at `2025-11-24T13:16:45` Pacific (21:16:45 UTC). It returned the same next window as the unbroken chain, `2025-12-12 20:39:07`.

`yarn test` still hasn't run because of the database hostname lookup failure from earlier. The `crawl_start_overlap_minutes` swap is still waiting on your go-ahead.

content.text:
`offset` isn't a ShipStation parameter. It's ours: an index into the 500 orders we already fetched. `page` is ShipStation's own `page` query param. Both are explained in `.claude/references/shipstation/api-summary.md`, under "`get_orders` — slice bulk-edited pages per task via an offset token", and in the comment at `integration.py:494`.

- **`page`** handles more than 500 orders sharing one `modifyDate` second. Re-querying from that second would return the same 500, so the token keeps the same second and asks ShipStation for its next page within it.
- **`offset`** handles pages full of old shipped orders. Any order created more than 7 days before `start` misses the shipment prefetch and needs its own `shipments` and `fulfillments` calls. A bulk edit once re-stamped `modifyDate` on about 200k old orders, so every page was 500 of these: about 1000 calls at v1's 40 requests a minute, longer than a task lives. The task was reclaimed before it ever saved a new cursor, so the crawl never moved. Now one call processes at most `SHIPSTATION_GET_ORDERS_HISTORICAL_CHUNK_SIZE` (50, `config.py:1206`) of those orders. It then returns the same `{modify_date, page}` plus the `offset` of the next unprocessed order. A crash loses at most one slice. This came from [TRA-2110](https://linear.app/trackstar-hq/issue/TRA-2110) and #5477.

Normal pages have no old orders, so they finish in one call with `offset` 0.

That api-summary section also says "`latest_data` advances only when the whole crawl drains", which this change makes untrue. I'll update that line when we're ready to commit.

content.text:
Your reading was right: the page should only be bumped when the modify date stays the same, and that's what the code did. `next_page` was only `page + 1` inside the `last_second == modify_start_str` case, so `"modify_date": last_second` was the unchanged second there. It needed a second read to see that, though. It's now three explicit branches:

1. **Whole page in the start second:** token `{modify_start_str, page + 1}`.
2. **Last second is after `start` and before `end`:** `next_start = last_second_dt`.
3. **Last second is at or before `start`** (the first loop's buffer) **or at `end`:** token `{last_second, page 1}`.

I kept your rename to `page`.

One side effect of your edits: `shipment_start_date` is back to `start - 7d` on every call instead of being saved on the first loop. After `next_start` moves `start` forward, the cutoff moves with it. But the shipment and fulfillment maps were only built once, on the first loop, from the original `start - 7d`. So orders the prefetch already covered, created between the old cutoff and the new one, get treated as old and trigger their own shipment and fulfillment lookups, and they count against the 50-order slice. The data stays correct, but a long backfill makes more of the slow per-order calls the further it gets. If that revert was deliberate, it's fine. If not, I'd restore `self.shipment_start_date`.

            # buffer to catch orders shipstation's api is slow to index

        page = 1

            page = page_token["page"]
            offset = page_token["offset"]

        pacific_start = modify_start_dt.astimezone(pytz.timezone("US/Pacific"))
        modify_start_str = pacific_start.strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S")

I restored `self.shipment_start_date`: it's set once on the first loop (`integration.py:365`), and every call reads it (`:415`).

When the crawl moves to `next_start`, `first_loop` is False. The crawler sets `first_loop = False` after the first `get_and_submit` and never sets it back (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:414`). The `next_start` branch (`:549-559`) only changes `start` and resets the token to `"default"`, so one task never repeats the buffer, the warehouse load or the shipment prefetch.

`first_loop` is True again only when a new task picks the crawl up, such as a resume after a crash or a reclaimed task. That task starts from the saved `latest_data`, which the last `next_start` advanced. It rebuilds the maps from that start, applies the 2h buffer once, and resets `shipment_start_date` to match.

I also noticed you dropped `not self.in_perm_validator()` from the full-page check. With `page_size = 1` there, the permission validator's page is always full, so it will now return a `next_start` or a token. That's harmless if the validator only makes one call and ignores both, but I haven't checked.

def handler(event, context):
    timeout = LAMBDA_SERVICES["permission-validator"]["timeout"] - 5
    with LambdaContextManager(event, context, timeout=timeout):
        for record in event.get("Records", []):
            msg = json.loads(record["body"])
            auth_code = msg["auth_code"]
            integration_type = msg["integration_type"]
            integration_name = msg["integration_name"]
            function_name = msg["function_name"]

            logger.updateConfig(
                {
                    "integration_name": integration_name,
                    "function_name": function_name,
                }
            )

            auth_code_row = get_auth_code_row(auth_code)

            app_integration_secret = auth_code_row["integration_secret"]
            raw_integration_secret = app_decrypt(app_integration_secret)
            additional_fields = auth_code_row["additional_fields"]

            integration_file = get_integration_file(integration_name, integration_type)
            integration = integration_file.Integration(
                integration_secret=raw_integration_secret,
                auth_code=auth_code,
                connection_additional_fields=additional_fields,
            )
            resource_type = function_to_resource_map[integration_type][function_name]
            resource = resource_type(integration)

            failed_urls = []
            blocked = False
            failed_to_test = False
            timed_out = False
            # the context manager owns SIGALRM for the whole invocation, so hand it back
            outer_handler = signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, raise_get_timeout)
            outer_remaining = signal.alarm(PERMISSION_VALIDATOR_GET_TIMEOUT)
            get_started_at = time.time()
            try:
                # same setup the crawler gives the function; without it a browser
                # carrier has no session and every validation records failed_to_test
                with integration.crawl_scope(resource):
                    resource.make_perm_call()
            except PermissionValidationTimeout as exc:
                logger.error(format_exception(exc))
                timed_out = True
                failed_to_test = True
            except (PermissionsException, InvalidCredentialsException) as exc:
                logger.error(format_exception(exc))
                blocked = True
                if isinstance(exc, InvalidCredentialsException):
                    url = "-"
                elif isinstance(exc, PermissionsException):
                    url = exc.url
                else:
                    raise Exception("improperly handled exception!")
                failed_urls.append(url)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error(
                    f"Non-Connection Error in permissions validation: {format_exception(e)}"
                )
                failed_to_test = True
            else:
                api_call_errors = integration.api_call_errors
                for error in api_call_errors.values():
                    if error:
                        failed_urls.append(error.url)
            finally:
                signal.alarm(0)
                signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, outer_handler)
                if outer_remaining:
                    get_elapsed = int(time.time() - get_started_at)
                    signal.alarm(max(1, outer_remaining - get_elapsed))

            column_dict = {
                "implemented": True,
                "failed_urls": failed_urls,
                "blocked": blocked,
                "failed_to_test": failed_to_test,
                "timed_out": timed_out,
            }
            update_auth_code_column(auth_code, resource.name(), column_dict)

        return {"status": "success", "message": "permission validation completed"}

content.text:
No. With `crawl_start_overlap_minutes`, the third case and `modify_date` both stay. Your other two questions:

**When the overlap applies.** Once per task, not once per backfill. `crawl_task` subtracts it when the task starts (`celery_tasks/crawler.py:302`). Moving to `next_start` inside the task sets `start_time_dt = next_start` directly (`:557-558`), with no overlap. A new task applies it again, whether that's a resume after a crash, a reclaimed task or the next scheduled crawl. It subtracts it from whatever start the scheduler hands over (`current_crawl_start`, otherwise `latest_data`, `lambda_handlers/scheduler.py:111-118`). So a backfill that resumes mid-way re-reads 2h once per resume, not once per window.

That's the same as the current code. Our buffer is gated on `first_loop`, and `first_loop` is True at the start of every task. It is the right behavior: each new task is a fresh read that could hit ShipStation's indexing lag. Limiting it to the very first loop of the backfill would need crawler changes, and I don't think it's worth it.

**`next_start` enforcement.** Yes. `crawler.py:474` raises unless `current_start_dt < next_start <= end_time_dt`. `current_start_dt` is the start without the overlap (`:386`), but `get_orders` receives the start with the overlap on a task's first loop. So with the overlap, the check in `get_orders` would have to be `start + overlap < last_second_dt` when `first_loop`, or the crawler raises.

**Why `modify_date` still can't go.** A `{page, offset}` token only makes sense relative to the second it was counted from. On a resume, the crawler passes `window start - 2h`:

- **First window:** `current_crawl_start` is the original start, and subtracting 2h reproduces the same anchor. This case works.
- **Any later window:** the anchor was `next_start` = X with no overlap, but the resume passes X - 2h. Page N now lands on different orders.

`get_orders` can't tell those two cases apart, so the token has to say where it was counted from. The third case also remains: a full page that ends inside the 2h buffer can't become `next_start`, so it needs a token pointing at that second.

So switching to the overlap would be mostly cosmetic: the standard knob instead of `timedelta(hours=2)` in the function, but it adds the `+ overlap` check and simplifies nothing else. I'd keep the current code.

While checking the resume path, I looked at the one place outside ShipStation that reads a saved token, the stale-schedule marker (`lambda_handlers/stale_schedule_marker.py:497-511`). It only runs for ShipHero, so the dict token doesn't affect it.

content.text:
No: gating the 2h on "first loop and no token" doesn't let `modify_date` go. That gate is effectively what already happens, since a token replaces the start. The first call's tokens are counted from `start - 2h`, and nothing tells the next call in the same window, or a resumed task, that the buffer was applied. So `modify_date` stays, and I've left it in.

Checking this turned up a bug in the branch, which I've fixed. The crawler already applies ShipStation's default 5-minute overlap (`BaseIntegration.py:98`) before calling `get_orders`. On a task's first loop, `get_orders` got `S - 5min` but the crawler checks `next_start` against the plain `S` (`crawler.py:386,474`). A full first page ending in `(S - 5min, S]` would have returned a `next_start` the crawler rejects with `next_start ... is not inside the remaining crawl range`, and the crawl would have failed the same way on every retry.

The fix, since it needs the overlap either way:
- **`crawl_start_overlap_minutes = 120`** on the ShipStation integration, replacing the in-function `timedelta(hours=2)`. The crawler applies it once per task. It doesn't re-apply when moving to `next_start`, which gives the "only on first loop" behavior. None of the other ShipStation functions use `start`, so only orders are affected.
- **`window_start`** is `start + overlap` on the first loop and plain `start` after that. The `next_start` check uses it, so it matches what the crawler enforces. The third case (a full page ending at or before `window_start`) still returns a token.

A dry-run `yarn crawl` from 2025-08-21 ran 3 pages of 500 through the real crawler with no `next_start` errors. `yarn test` still can't run here because of the database hostname lookup failure, so it needs a run where the DB resolves.

content.text:
You're right that `start` already includes the overlap. The catch is that the crawler checks `next_start` against a different number than the one it hands you.

`crawl_task` keeps two starts (`celery_tasks/crawler.py`):
- `start_time_dt` = saved start − 120 min. That's what `get_orders` receives as `start` (`:302`).
- `current_start_dt` = the saved start with no overlap (`:386`). The `next_start` check uses this one (`:474`): `current_start_dt < next_start`.

Example: `latest_data` is 10:00.
- `get_orders` is called with `start` = 08:00.
- The first full page's last order is at 09:30.
- Checking against `start`, 09:30 is after 08:00, so we'd return `next_start = 09:30`.
- The crawler compares 09:30 with 10:00, finds it isn't later, and raises.

The check is there to stop `latest_data` from moving backward. Returning 09:30 would set `latest_data` to 09:30, earlier than the 10:00 we'd already reached. The overlap is for re-reading old orders, not for giving up progress.

So on the first loop, `get_orders` has to compare against 10:00, and it only knows 08:00. `start + overlap` gets back to 10:00, and that's all `window_start` does. After the first `next_start`, the crawler passes the new start with no overlap, so `start` and `window_start` are the same.

The page that ended at 09:30 isn't lost. It returns a token anchored at 09:30, the third case, and the next page usually ends after 10:00 and becomes a normal `next_start`.

If you'd rather `get_orders` not do this arithmetic, the alternative is to pass the no-overlap start into the integration. But that's a crawler change for every integration, so I'd keep `window_start`.

content.text:
You're right that at most one can be set. The code never sets both. There are four outcomes:

| Situation | `next_token` | `next_start` |
|---|---|---|
| Page not full (crawl is done) | None | None |
| Full page, all in one second | `{same second, page + 1, offset 0}` | None |
| Full page, last second between `current_start_dt` and `end` | None | last second |
| Full page, last second at or before `current_start_dt` (or at `end`) | `{last second, page 1, offset 0}` | None |

The first-pass branches (`:398-420`) set at most one of `page_next_token` and `page_next_start`. The slicing at `:526-536` then decides whether to use them.

**What `slice_end` does.** It walks the page from `offset` and stops just before the 51st old shipped order, the kind that needs its own shipment and fulfillment calls. `work_orders = orders[offset:slice_end]` is what this call processes.

- **`slice_end < len(orders)`:** the page isn't finished. It returns only the offset token, `{same modify_date, same page, offset: slice_end}`, and forces `next_start = None`. The window can't move forward while orders on this page are still unprocessed, because that would skip them.
- **`slice_end == len(orders)`:** the page is done, so it hands on whichever of `page_next_token` or `page_next_start` the first part picked.

The next call with the offset token re-fetches the same page, processes the next slice, and runs the same first-pass logic. Only the call that finishes the page can emit `next_start`.

One more case I checked: a crash in the middle of the slices. The resumed task gets `first_loop=True` and a start with the overlap applied. That gives `current_start_dt = start + overlap`, the value the crawler checks against, so the final slice's `next_start` still passes.

The crawler also enforces the rule. `validate_crawl` asserts `next_token must be None when next_start is set` (`resources/base_resource.py:700`), so a bug here would fail loudly rather than be silently ignored.

# Query Datadog (Trackstar crawler logs)

Crawl logs are in Datadog under `service:crawler*`. Get tags vs attributes right first: the wrong syntax returns zero rows, not an error.

## Tags vs attributes (read this first)

- **Tags** are infrastructure and pipeline metadata, written `key:value` with **no `@`**:
  - `service:crawler*` (the `*` covers `crawler-service-prod` etc.)
  - `status:error` (log level: `error`, `warn`, `info`)
  - `env:prod`
  - `host:...`, `source:...`
- **Attributes** are structured fields logged on each crawl, written `@key:value` **with `@`**:
  - `@connection_id:<id>`
  - `@function:<get_orders|get_inventory|…>`
  - `@integration_name:<shiphero|fba|…>`
  - `@org_id:<org_…>`
  - `@sync_job_id:<id>`

**The `@` matters.** `@connection_id:abc` is the attribute; `connection_id:abc` without `@` is read as a tag and matches nothing. The reverse fails too: `service` is a tag, so `@service:crawler*` is wrong. Fields logged on the crawl record take `@`; pipeline fields (`service`, `status`, `env`, `host`) do not. If a query returns zero rows, check this first.

## The standard crawler query

**Start broad.** Don't pre-filter to errors: you lose the most useful context (crawls that are running, the shape of the pattern, intermittent vs constant).

```
service:crawler* env:prod @integration_name:<name> @function:<function>
```

Run it over the staleness window (next section). Only after seeing the whole picture, narrow with follow-up queries:
- add `status:error` to isolate failures,
- add `@connection_id:<id>` to scope to one connection,
- add a literal error string in quotes (e.g. `"Crawl killed"`, `"rate limit"`, `"KeyError"`).

Every investigation and PR starts from this same query; narrower cuts go in as separate links when they help.

## Time window — pin the start

Never accept Datadog's default of the last 15 minutes; a schedule may have gone stale weeks ago. Times are epoch **milliseconds**:
- `from_ts` = the schedule's `latest_data` (when it went stale).
- Leave the end at now. Interactive search defaults `to` to now, so omit it. Only the **shareable URL** below needs an explicit `to_ts` (now in epoch ms) so its window stays fixed.
- If `latest_data` is very old, you may cap the lookback (e.g. 15-30 days) to keep the query fast. Say that you capped it.

Agent context: `datadog:search_datadog_logs` takes `query`, `from`, and `start_at` for pagination (`to` defaults to now).

```
datadog:search_datadog_logs(
  query="service:crawler* env:prod @integration_name:<name> @function:<function>",
  from="<staleness onset>"
)
```

## What the patterns tell you

| Pattern | Likely meaning |
|---------|----------------|
| Burst of 401/403 after days of success | Credentials rotated by the integration vendor |
| Consistent 429 / "rate limit" / "throttle" | Vendor rate limit; crawl can't complete its budget |
| "Crawl killed" clustered around deploy times | Infra redeploy, not an API issue (check deploy history first) |
| Timeout on one function but not others | Specific endpoint slow or response too large |
| Exception + stack trace | Code bug — read the traceback, find the function + line |
| `page=` climbing into the thousands in a tight window | Runaway pagination loop in the crawler |
| Crawls completing but `latest_data` flat | Cursor not advancing, or no new vendor data |

## Building a shareable Datadog link (PRs / Linear cards)

Put the standard query and the pinned window into this URL:

    https://app.datadoghq.com/logs?query=service%3Acrawler%2A%20env%3Aprod%20%40integration_name%3A<name>%20%40function%3A<function>&cols=host%2Cservice&messageDisplay=inline&storage=hot&stream_sort=desc&viz=stream&live=false&from_ts=<latest_data_ms>&to_ts=<now_ms>

Fill in `<name>` and `<function>`, and put real epoch-ms integers in `from_ts` and `to_ts`. Leave no `<…>` or `…` in it, or the link falls back to the last-15-minutes default.

Put it in the body as a bare `[Datadog](url)` link on its own line, formatted per `.claude/rules/communications.md`: never inside backticks or a code fence (it renders as literal text). Don't use a raw HTML anchor either; the PR-creation pipeline strips it to bare text.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Datadog__analyze_datadog_logs
entries.description: Analyze Datadog logs using SQL. Runs against a virtual 'logs' table filtered by your search query. Good for aggregations, counts, group-bys, or peeking at recent logs with LIMIT. To discover custom attributes for extra_columns, first call search_datadog_logs with extra_fields. If a query times out, try a shorter time range. MUST load the datadog/ddsql skill before calling this tool.

extra_columns.description: Extend the logs table with additional typed columns. To discover available attributes, call search_datadog_logs with extra_fields (e.g. ['*'] or ['http*']), then declare them here. Key translation from search response keys to extra_columns names: strip the bucket prefix and prepend '@' — `custom.X` → `{name: "@X"}`, `attributes.X` → `{name: "@X"}`, `error.X` → `{name: "@error.X"}`; tags from the `tags:` list use bare names without '@' — e.g. tag `team:foo` → `{name: "team"}`. Never pass the raw response-prefixed form (e.g. never `custom.X` or `attributes.X`). Supported types: varchar, bigint, decimal, boolean, timestamp, array<varchar>, array<bigint>, array<decimal>, array<boolean>, array<timestamp>.

name.description: Column name in the SQL virtual table.

filter.description: Datadog search query to filter logs before SQL analysis. When relevant services are known, prefer filtering by service name or prefix. Broad queries are fine for discovery or cross-service questions. Use key:value for tags/facets (e.g. 'service:nginx', 'env:prod'), '@' prefix for raw attributes (e.g. '@http.status_code:[400 TO 499]'). Examples: 'service:nginx status:error', 'env:(production OR test) AND -version:beta', 'service:web* foo'. Tip: '(source:foo OR service:foo)' if unsure which field. For severe issues: 'status:(critical OR alert OR emergency)'.

from.description: Start of time window. ISO 8601, Unix epoch ms, or relative ('now-1h').

indexes.description: Restrict to specific log indexes (e.g. ['main', 'pci']). Default: ['*'] (all).

sql_query.description: SQL against the 'logs' table. Examples: 'SELECT count(*) FROM logs', 'SELECT service, count(*) FROM logs GROUP BY service ORDER BY count(*) DESC', 'SELECT status, count(*) FROM logs GROUP BY status', 'SELECT DATE_TRUNC(\'hour\', timestamp) as hour, count(*) FROM logs GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC(\'hour\', timestamp)'. Default columns: timestamp (timestamp), host (string), service (string), env (string), version (string), status (string), message (string); add more via extra_columns. DDSQL (Datadog SQL) is a PostgreSQL subset: every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY, SELECT aliases cannot be reused in WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING (repeat the full expression instead, e.g., GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('hour', timestamp) not GROUP BY hour), and only declared table columns may be referenced. Use the -> operator or json_extract_path_text (cast as needed) for JSON access. Avoid unsupported constructs like ANY(), ->>, QUALIFY, information_schema, and current_timestamp. Column names containing special characters like '@' must be quoted (e.g., SELECT "@foo" FROM logs). TIME FILTERING: the virtual table already contains only events within the from/to time window — never add WHERE timestamp >= ... in SQL. INTERVAL and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are not supported and will cause query errors.

storage_tier.description: Storage type: 'indexes' (default, hot only), 'flex_and_indexes' (Flex + hot). online-archives and cloudprem not supported.

intent.description: Briefly describe the wider context task, and why this tool was chosen. Omit argument values, PII/secrets. Use English.

to.description: End of time window. Same formats as 'from'.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Datadog__search_datadog_logs
entries.description: Search and retrieve raw log entries or log patterns. Do NOT use for counting or aggregations — use analyze_datadog_logs instead. Best for: viewing raw logs, discovering patterns (use_log_patterns=true), and discovering custom attributes via extra_fields for use as extra_columns in analyze_datadog_logs. Response shape (when extra_fields is set, output is YAML): three buckets — (1) top-level fields like env/host/service queried bare (`env:prod`); (2) `attributes:` map with source-prefixed keys — `custom.X` and `attributes.X` are queried as `@X` (strip the bucket prefix), but `error.X` keeps its prefix as `@error.X` because `error` is a real top-level attribute; (3) `tags:` list of `key:value` strings queried bare. Load the datadog/logs skill for the full key-translation table.

clustering_pattern_field.description: Log field used for clustering logs with similar values when use_log_patterns is true. Can cluster on any attribute or tag present in the logs. Consider '@error.message', '@errorMessage', '@error' or '@error.stack' when investigating error logs. Default: 'message'.

extra_fields.description: Extra attributes/tags to include. Use bare names without '@' or prefix (e.g., 'duration', not '@duration' or 'custom.duration'). Supports wildcards ('experiments*', '*' for all). The response shows attribute keys with a display prefix (custom.X, error.X); that prefix signals the translation: custom.X → @X, error.X → @error.X in extra_columns. Load the datadog/logs skill for the full translation table.

from.description: Start of the time range. Accepts ISO 8601 (e.g. '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z' or '2024-01-01'), Unix timestamp (seconds or milliseconds), or relative (e.g. 'now-1h', 'now-7d', 'now'). Default: now-1h.

indexes.description: Restrict to specific log indexes (e.g. ['main', 'pci']). Default: ['*'] (all).

limit.description: Optional maximum number of logs or patterns to return (1-1000). If omitted, results are bounded only by max_tokens.

max_tokens.description: Max tokens in the response. Hard cap: 20000 (values above are clamped, not rejected).

pattern_group_by.description: Only used when use_log_patterns=true. Fields/tags to group patterns by (e.g. ['service', '@env']). Can group by any attribute or tag present in the logs. Each returned pattern will be scoped to a unique combination of these fields, and their values surface in the 'groups' column. Default: no grouping (patterns aggregate across all values).

query.description: Datadog search query. When relevant services are known, prefer filtering by service name or prefix. Broad queries are fine for discovery or cross-service questions. Common tags: service, env, host, source. Prefix raw attributes with '@'. Examples: 'service:nginx status:error', '@http.status_code:[400 TO 499]', 'env:(production OR test) AND -version:beta', 'service:web* foo', '"foo bar"'. Tip: '(source:foo OR service:foo)' if unsure which field. Severe issues: 'status:(critical OR alert OR emergency)'.

storage_tier.description: Storage type. 'flex_and_indexes' (Flex + hot), 'online_archives_and_indexes' (archive + hot). Default: hot only.

intent.description: Briefly describe the wider context task, and why this tool was chosen. Omit argument values, PII/secrets. Use English.

to.description: End of the time range. Accepts ISO 8601 (e.g. '2024-01-01T00:00:00Z' or '2024-01-01'), Unix timestamp (seconds or milliseconds), or relative (e.g. 'now-1h', 'now-7d', 'now'). Default: now.

use_log_patterns.description: When true, returns clusters of logs with similar messages instead of raw logs.

+## A naive datetime *filter* is evaluated against the vendor's clock, not ours

+- The localization problem has a request-side twin that is easier to miss than the response-side one above. When a list endpoint filters on a naive `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss` string, the vendor compares it to its own wall clock. Send a UTC `now()` as the upper bound to a vendor running UTC+8 and the window ends eight hours in that vendor's past, so the most recent records are silently outside it.

+- When it bites: the crawl returns `total: 0` or a short page and looks like "nothing new" rather than an error, so it survives review and only surfaces as a customer reporting missing recent records. A wide backfill window hides it completely — it only appears once the window's upper bound approaches now, which is every incremental crawl.

+- How to handle: probe it rather than reasoning about it. Query a window whose upper bound is `now()` in UTC against records you know exist, then the same window shifted by the vendor's offset; if the first returns nothing and the second returns them, the filter is local-time. Do not assume it is uniform across the vendor: on the same host, endpoint families can differ, so confirm per family. And rule out read-back/index lag first (see the entry above) — a freshly written record invisible to *any* time window but findable by id is lag, not clock skew, and shifting the window there makes things worse.

# Code style (pokedex Python)

The always-on subset, consolidated from CLAUDE.md and `integration-patterns.md` "Code style". Full reviewer checklist (incl. advisory / new-build-only items like `while True`, guard clauses, inline dict values): `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Code style".

- **No docstrings, with two exceptions.** Pokedex code is self-documenting. Both exceptions are where the docstring is published text, not a comment: `api.py` endpoint handlers, whose docstring is the endpoint's OpenAPI summary and description (the rollout pushes that spec to Mintlify and Svix, so it is the public API docs, and every public endpoint carries one); Alembic migration modules under `migrations/versions/`, which keep the generated header (title, `Revision ID`, `Revises`, `Create Date`) plus a line of rationale when the schema change is not obvious from the operations. Nothing under `integrations/`, `utils/`, `resources/`, or `actions/` has one.
- **Default to no comment; when in doubt, delete.** A comment exists only when the change is not obvious from the code alone. If the code, a variable name, or the error message beside it already says it, the comment is noise — delete it rather than polish it. That covers narration ("sum the quantities per sku"), section labels, and anything restating an assert or a raise.
- **Comments: lowercase, ≤2 lines, why not what.** Vendor quirks, surprising invariants, non-obvious couplings. Vendor field names keep their original casing inside a lowercase comment (`DeliveryNotes` stays `DeliveryNotes`) — lowercasing them breaks the reference. The ceiling yields only when a genuinely non-obvious vendor data model or a disambiguating example needs the room and nothing shorter carries it. The same ceiling applies to raised error messages — a `PokedexException` says what went wrong and what to do in a line or two, not a paragraph.
- **ELI5, no jargon.** Write it the way you'd say it out loud to an engineer new to the codebase: plain words any SWE understands cold, in one read. No noun-stacks ("multi-lot pick collision"), no arrow chains (`x → y → z`), no model-speak ("ensure correctness", "for clarity", "leverage"), no clever compression that needs decoding ("must not look like it did"). "with no batch number, picks from different batches get combined here, so we can't keep a single expiry date" beats "blank-batch multi-lot picks collapse under the package uniqueness key, dropping the expiry anchor".
- **Comments are self-contained.** Never reference `api-summary.md`, any `.claude/...` file, doctrine vocabulary ("tier-3", "shallow-fix", "per integration-patterns"), or the authoring agent. A reader at HEAD with only this file open must understand it.
- **Comments never name** customer orgs, the source integration a pattern was copied from, or observation dates — those leak or rot. The ban is on customers: naming the integration's own vendor inside its own files is normal. Rich rationale (customer, pattern source, load-bearing dates) lives in `api-summary.md` "Field-mapping decisions". Exception: vendor/3PL support-contact lines inside `support()` — naming contacts is that method's job.
- **Raise, don't `assert`.** Runtime error paths raise `PokedexException` (or the typed `create_*` exception helpers), never `assert` — asserts strip under `python -O` and carry no status or origin. `assert` belongs in tests only.
- **A package `__init__.py` that re-exports lists those names in `__all__`.** Re-exports are the point of the file, but every one of them reads as an unused import to the linter, so the list is what keeps it quiet and doubles as the package's public surface. Add a name in both places or the linter flags it again.
- **No `@property` on anything a subclass overrides.** A value an integration can change is a plain method, so every call site shows it's dispatched rather than read off the instance. `@property` is still fine for something defined once and never overridden (`staging_key`, `bucket`). Name a boolean method for how it reads at the call site — `uses_browserbase()`, not `use_browserbase()`.
- **No `ABC` / `@abstractmethod`.** A base class declares a method subclasses must supply by raising `NotImplementedError` in the body, with a short message saying what the subclass owes. That's the one pattern used everywhere else, and on integrations it's load-bearing: `BaseIntegration.is_implemented` reads a method's source looking for that raise to decide which functions an integration supports, so an abstract stub would be read as implemented and get scheduled.
- **UPPER_CASE names are module-level only.** A constant-style value scoped inside a function is a lowercase local like any other; capitals are reserved for module-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor tunables).
- **No leading-underscore "private" names** on methods, attributes, or locals. Underscore privacy isn't enforced here and signals nothing. If a class helper needs `self` it's a method; if not, hoist it module-level; if used once, inline it. (Dunders like `__init__` are exempt.)
- **Error-driven: avoid `.get()` — on vendor-response reads.** Loud failures (a `KeyError` during `yarn crawl`) are how we learn real API behavior. `.get(field, default)` on a vendor response is allowed only after observing the field is genuinely sometimes-absent. Nullable is not optional: a key the vendor always sends but sometimes nulls is read with a direct index (plus an `or` fallback when a default is needed) — `.get()` there misstates the contract by implying the key can be missing. The rule does not cover reads where absence is the normal, documented case — optional fields of a validated write payload in `create_*`/`update_*` methods, marshmallow `query_data` in API handlers (absent optional params are omitted from the dict), and our own state attributes that most rows don't carry — there `.get()` is the convention and is self-documenting. Comment a `.get()` only when the absence is surprising (the contract says the field should be there and observation proved otherwise: `# vendor returns null for unfulfilled orders`); a `.get()` on a documented-optional field needs no comment.
- **No list/dict comprehensions in integration code.** Use multi-line `for` loops with named intermediates — comprehensions are opaque under `pdb`.
- **No `logger.info` / `print` in integration code** (carrier is the documented exception — its async/queued flows justify checkpoint logging). Every other type stays quiet: Datadog spans + connection-error rows are the observability surface; `logger.warning`/`error` only for genuinely surprising, actionable states.
- **Platform constants live in `config.py`.** Feature modules `import config`; don't scatter `os.environ.get`. Integration-level constants (status maps, page sizes, vendor base URLs, per-vendor tunables) stay in the integration's own module — they're hard to unify across vendors and don't belong in the shared config.
- **Favor simplicity over cleverness — and the smallest fix that addresses the root cause.** A fix that adds new mechanisms (a helper, a wrapper, a retry layer, config) where editing an existing line suffices is overengineered and gets rejected in review. Before inventing a new shape, check how neighboring integrations already solve the same problem and match it. The same bar applies to edge cases: a narrow race or double-failure edge that self-corrects on the next cycle (or whose outcome is still correct for the user) is documented — or made observable with a log line — not engineered around with new state machines or guards.

- **Reuse the codebase's words; never coin a verb.** A name is found, not composed: before naming a function, helper, constant, status value, or table, grep for how neighbors name the same operation on the same kind of thing (`rg -n 'def \w+_<noun>\b'`, `rg -n 'def \w+_row\b'`) and pick from the verbs that come back; the search is by object, never by a list of verbs, because a list is itself a vocabulary that drifts. Dynamo row helpers are `create_ / get_ / update_ / store_ / delete_<thing>_row`. Under `integrations/`, data-function and action names come from the resource and action contracts, so there is nothing to choose. A status string is the word the API's error text uses for that state (`unconfirmed` when the 409 says "could not be confirmed"), so the row, the log line, and the error read the same. A word from one recent feature is not established vocabulary; count its uses across the repo before adopting it. Payments, ops, and distributed-systems jargon (`settle`, `claim`, `release`, `landed`, `in flight`, `ambiguous`, `reconcile`) is a coined verb here unless the grep shows it already carries that meaning in this codebase. Say what the code does in words the code already uses: `mark_<row>_succeeded`, `store_write_ids_for_replay`, `write_may_have_reached_vendor`.
- **Comments and error messages use the code's own names.** A comment names the function, status, and field exactly as the code spells them and describes the mechanism in the same verbs. A comment that introduces a second vocabulary for the thing beside it is rewritten in the code's words or deleted.

## Running code & tests
- **Tests: only `yarn test` with filters.** Never `python -m pytest` or raw `pytest`. Scopes/markers: `.claude/skills/run-scripts/guides/test.md`.
- **Ad-hoc Python: `uv run python3`.** Never raw `python3`/`python` — dependencies resolve through `uv`.

# Write safety — never touch production vendor data

Full rules: `.claude/references/integration-patterns.md` "Write safety". The always-on core:

- **Write methods** — `create_*`, `update_*`, `cancel_*`, `delete_*`, `adjust_*`, `refund_*` (anything that mutates vendor state) — are gated by **`allow_writes()` on the test class** (defined in `test/integrations/base_test.py`, defaults `True`; read by `write_and_validate`, which skips every write test when `False`).
- **Any connection that is not writes-safe** — prod-as-test, customer-owned, or unlabeled — the test class **MUST** override `allow_writes(self): return False`. Without the override, write tests fire against the vendor.
- **File-based integrations: `allow_file_archive()` on the test class gates the archive step** (defined in `test/integrations/base_test.py`, defaults `False`; crawl tests patch out `archive_staged_files` unless the class opts in). Archiving consumes files off the vendor's server, and on a prod or shared server that starves the customer's own crawls. Return `True` only for a sandbox or test server we're allowed to drain, per `test_account()`.
- **Don't restate the writes-safe default.** On a writes-safe connection, omit `allow_writes()` rather than writing `return True`. An explicit `True` earns its place only as a deliberate authorization record — a prod-as-test account where writes were confirmed safe — paired with a `test_account()` that says so and why.
- **`test_account()` is the human-readable rationale** for that value: `"<requesting org> <env> · <ownership> · <write-safety> · <linear-ticket>"`. The leading token is the trackstar customer org that requested the build — not `test-org-id`, not the vendor name. `test_account()` and `allow_writes()` must agree (`writes-unsafe` ↔ returns `False`). A `test-*` connection_id does **not** imply writes-safe.
- **Never run a write operation against a vendor API while investigating or validating**, regardless of account safety. HTTP method is **not** the gate — SOAP and GraphQL reads are POST; the operation's *effect on vendor data* is. Default to read-only paths: `yarn crawl` dry-run and documented read endpoints. Never change `allow_writes()` / `test_account()` to flip write-safety as a shortcut.
